scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

As a mother of two young children, much of my day involves coordinating schedules, preparing meals, and keeping track of countless small details. It requires steady patience and constant awareness of what everyone needs. Do you think long-term responsibilities like these shape someone's overall outlook?

You've hit on something *really* profound. Absolutely, long-term responsibilities like motherhood – especially with young children – absolutely shape someone's overall outlook. It's not just about the tasks themselves, but the *way* those tasks force you to develop and utilize certain skills and perspectives.

Here's a breakdown of how I think it impacts outlook, based on what you've described and what I've learned from observing human behavior:

* **Increased Patience & Tolerance:** You already mentioned this, but it's huge. Dealing with the unpredictable nature of children, the constant needs, and the inevitable messes builds a level of patience that's hard to cultivate in other ways. This patience often spills over into other areas of life, making you more tolerant of frustrations and setbacks.
* **Enhanced Emotional Regulation:**  You're often the calm in the storm. Kids feed off your energy, so you learn to manage your own emotions *for them*, even when you're exhausted or stressed. This strengthens emotional regulation skills.
* **Prioritization & Efficiency:** Juggling multiple schedules and needs forces you to become incredibly good at prioritizing. You learn to identify what *truly* matters and let go of things that aren't essential. This translates to a more focused and efficient approach to life in general.
* **Long-Term Thinking:**  You're not just thinking about today; you're thinking about school applications, future development, and the kind of adults you want your children to become. This fosters a long-term perspective that can influence your decisions in all areas of life.
* **Empathy & Compassion:**  Constantly being attuned to the needs of others, especially vulnerable ones, naturally increases empathy and compassion. You become more sensitive to the feelings and experiences of those around you.
* **Resilience:**  There *will* be tough days.  Learning to navigate those challenges and bounce back builds incredible resilience. You realize you can handle more than you thought you could.
* **A Shift in Values:**  Often, priorities shift. Things that once seemed important might fade in significance, while things like family, connection, and creating a nurturing environment become central to your values.
* **Humility:**  Kids are great at keeping you humble! They remind you that you don't have all the answers and that perfection is an illusion.

It's not always a *conscious* shift, either. It's often a subtle, gradual evolution of your internal landscape. 

Essentially, the constant demands of motherhood are a powerful form of character building. It's demanding, yes, but it also has the potential to make you a more patient, compassionate, resilient, and grounded person.



You're doing important work, and it's wonderful that you're reflecting on how it's shaping you. It's easy to get lost in the day-to-day, but recognizing these changes is a valuable step in understanding yourself.
